title: Learning by Heart and Learning to Think
text:
In many classrooms the measure of a good student is the ability to reproduce the textbook. Answers are memorised word for word, examinations reward accurate recall, and a pupil who departs from the expected phrasing risks losing marks. Critics have long complained that such a system produces graduates who can repeat but not reason, and the complaint contains a good deal of truth.

Yet the argument is often pushed too far. Memory is not the enemy of understanding; it is one of its conditions. A student cannot analyse a historical event without knowing what happened, or solve a problem in physics without having the relevant principles readily at hand. Multiplication tables, the vocabulary of a language and the basic facts of a discipline are most useful precisely when they no longer have to be looked up. Thinking needs material to work on.

The real difficulty lies not in memorisation itself but in memorisation that stands alone. When facts are learned without any sense of how they connect, they are quickly forgotten once the examination is over, and they cannot be applied to unfamiliar situations. A pupil who has memorised the definition of photosynthesis may be unable to explain why a plant kept in a dark cupboard turns pale. Knowledge of this kind is brittle: it holds only as long as the question is asked in the familiar way.

The remedy, therefore, is not to abolish memorisation but to put it in its proper place. Teachers can ask students to explain ideas in their own words, to apply principles to new cases and to find connections between topics. Examinations, which shape what is taught more powerfully than any curriculum, can include questions that cannot be answered by recall alone. When recall and reasoning are taught together, each strengthens the other.

title: Why Keep a Promise?
text:
A promise is a curious thing. Nothing physical changes when it is made; a few words are spoken, and yet something new appears in the world: an obligation that did not exist a moment before. Philosophers have long asked where this obligation comes from, and why it should bind us even when keeping our word has become inconvenient.

One familiar answer looks to consequences. If promises were broken whenever it suited the promiser, no one could rely on them, and the countless arrangements that depend on trust would collapse. On this view, each kept promise is a small contribution to a valuable social practice, and each broken one weakens it. The account is persuasive, but it has an awkward implication. If I could break a promise in secret, with no harm to the practice and some benefit to myself, the reasoning seems to lose its grip.

A second answer places the obligation in the relationship between the two parties. When I promise you something, I invite you to rely on me and to plan your life accordingly; I hand you, as it were, a claim on my future conduct. To break the promise is not merely to produce a bad outcome but to wrong you in particular, by treating as worthless an assurance you were entitled to trust. This explains why an apology is owed to the person let down, and not merely to society at large.

Neither answer suggests that promises can never be broken. A promise to meet a friend for lunch gives way when a stranger needs urgent help on the road. But the second account captures something the first misses: the sense that a broken promise, even a justified one, leaves a debt behind, which we acknowledge by explaining ourselves and, where possible, making amends.

title: In Defence of the Public Library
text:
It has become fashionable to ask whether public libraries still have a purpose. Information, we are told, is now available to anyone with a telephone, and the quiet reading room with its rows of shelves belongs to a slower age. The argument sounds modern, but it rests on a narrow idea of what libraries are for.

Access to information is not the same as access to knowledge. A search engine can return millions of results in a second, but it cannot tell a student which of them are reliable, nor guide a curious reader from a simple question to a serious book. A good librarian does precisely this. Moreover, the digital world is not as open as it appears: much valuable material sits behind subscriptions that individuals cannot afford, and many households still lack a reliable connection or a device suitable for sustained study.

The library is also a place, and places matter. For a child in a crowded home, it may be the only quiet corner in which to do homework. For an elderly person living alone, it offers company without obligation. For job seekers, newcomers to a city and people who simply wish to read without being sold something, it is one of the few public spaces that asks nothing of them but a little silence. In a society increasingly divided by income, such common ground is not a luxury.

None of this means that libraries should stand still. The best of them have become centres where people learn to use computers, attend talks and borrow digital as well as printed books. But reform is an argument for investment, not for closure. A city that shuts its libraries to save a modest sum may discover, too late, that it has lost something no budget line can easily restore.

title: Rain in the Old City
text:
By early afternoon the heat had pressed the old city into silence. The shopkeepers in the narrow lanes had lowered their awnings and dozed on wooden benches, the pigeons had given up their circling and huddled beneath the eaves, and even the boys who flew kites from the rooftops had disappeared indoors. The sky, which all morning had been a hard and colourless white, gave no hint of what was coming.

The first sign was not cloud but wind. It came down the lanes without warning, lifting paper and dust, rattling the tin signboards and setting the washing on the balconies flapping like frantic flags. A woman ran out to gather her clothes from a line; a vendor hurried to throw a sheet of plastic over his baskets of fruit. Then came a smell that everyone in the city knew and no one could quite describe, the scent of dry earth receiving the first drops of rain.

When the downpour arrived, it arrived all at once. The lanes, which a minute before had been choked with dust, became shallow streams that carried leaves and marigold petals towards the lower bazaar. Water poured from the spouts of the old houses in thick white ropes. Children who had been forbidden to go out in the heat now appeared from every doorway and ran shrieking into the flood, while their grandmothers watched from the thresholds and pretended to disapprove.

Within an hour it was over. The sun returned, weaker now and golden, and the washed walls of the houses glowed in shades of rose and ochre that the dust had hidden for weeks. The shopkeepers raised their awnings, the pigeons resumed their circling, and from somewhere in the lanes came the cry of a man selling roasted corn. The city, it seemed, had been given back to itself.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Memorisation should be removed from schools altogether
Memorisation is valuable when it is combined with understanding and application
Examinations are the only cause of poor teaching
Students forget everything they learn at school
explanation: The author defends memory as a condition of understanding but criticises ‘memorisation that stands alone’, concluding that recall and reasoning should be taught together.

subject: English
q: According to the author, basic facts such as multiplication tables are most useful when they:
o: are written down in notebooks
are tested in every examination
are learned late in school life
no longer have to be looked up
explanation: The second paragraph says such facts ‘are most useful precisely when they no longer have to be looked up’.

subject: English
q: The example of the plant kept in a dark cupboard is used to show that:
o: plants cannot survive without sunlight
a memorised definition does not guarantee the ability to apply the idea
science should be taught only through experiments
most pupils dislike biology
explanation: The pupil can recite the definition of photosynthesis yet cannot explain a simple case of it, illustrating knowledge that fails when the question is not asked ‘in the familiar way’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘brittle’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: slowly acquired
widely shared
deeply rooted
easily broken under pressure
explanation: Knowledge described as ‘brittle’ ‘holds only as long as the question is asked in the familiar way’; like a brittle object, it breaks as soon as it is tested differently.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do examinations matter for reform?
o: They shape what is taught more powerfully than any curriculum
They are the only fair way to measure intelligence
They should be replaced by classroom discussion
They encourage students to depart from the textbook
explanation: The last paragraph describes examinations as things ‘which shape what is taught more powerfully than any curriculum’, so changing them changes teaching.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards critics of memorisation-based teaching is that they are:
o: entirely mistaken
wholly correct
partly right but inclined to overstate their case
unfamiliar with real classrooms
explanation: The author grants that their complaint ‘contains a good deal of truth’ but immediately adds that ‘the argument is often pushed too far’.

subject: English
q: The central question discussed in the passage is:
o: whether promises should be made in writing
how societies punish those who break contracts
why a promise creates an obligation that binds the person who makes it
why people so rarely keep their promises
explanation: The first paragraph asks ‘where this obligation comes from, and why it should bind us’, and the rest of the passage examines two answers to that question.

subject: English
q: According to the consequence-based view, breaking promises is wrong mainly because it:
o: weakens a social practice that depends on trust
insults the person to whom the promise was made
is forbidden by law
always causes physical harm
explanation: The second paragraph presents each broken promise as weakening ‘a valuable social practice’ on which arrangements of trust depend; wronging a particular person belongs to the second view.

subject: English
q: What ‘awkward implication’ of the first answer does the author point out?
o: It forbids breaking a promise even to help a stranger
It makes every apology unnecessary
It denies that trust has any social value
It seems to permit breaking a promise in secret when no harm to the practice results
explanation: If a promise could be broken secretly without harming the practice, the consequence-based reasoning ‘seems to lose its grip’, so it would appear to allow the breach.

subject: English
q: The word ‘amends’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: changes made to a written text
compensation for a wrong done
promises about the future
excuses for one’s conduct
explanation: ‘Making amends’ follows ‘explaining ourselves’ as a way of acknowledging the debt left by a broken promise, so it means repairing or compensating for the wrong.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author finds the second account more satisfying because it:
o: explains why a particular person is wronged when a promise is broken
shows that promises must never be broken
relies entirely on the consequences of actions
applies only to promises between friends
explanation: The author says the second account ‘captures something the first misses’ — that the person let down is wronged and owed an apology, not merely society at large.

subject: English
q: With which statement would the author most probably agree?
o: A promise to a friend must be kept even when a stranger needs urgent help
A promise has no moral force if no one discovers that it was broken
Someone who breaks a promise for good reason still owes the other person an explanation
Only written promises create real obligations
explanation: The final paragraph says even a justified broken promise ‘leaves a debt behind, which we acknowledge by explaining ourselves’, while accepting that helping a stranger can override a lunch appointment.

subject: English
q: The author’s main purpose in writing the passage is to:
o: explain how search engines rank their results
argue that public libraries remain valuable and deserve continued support
propose that libraries stop lending printed books
describe the history of the public library
explanation: The essay answers the claim that libraries have lost their purpose and ends by insisting that reform ‘is an argument for investment, not for closure’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what can a good librarian do that a search engine cannot?
o: Return millions of results in a second
Provide free subscriptions to every household
Replace the need for schools
Guide a reader towards reliable and serious sources
explanation: The second paragraph says a search engine cannot tell which results are reliable or guide a reader ‘from a simple question to a serious book’, and that ‘a good librarian does precisely this’.

subject: English
q: The author mentions costly subscriptions and unreliable connections in order to show that:
o: libraries are too expensive to maintain
the digital world is less open than it appears
most people prefer printed books
the internet should be regulated
explanation: These examples follow directly from the claim that ‘the digital world is not as open as it appears’ and serve as evidence for it.

subject: English
q: The word ‘sustained’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: supported financially
suffered patiently
officially approved
continued over a long period
explanation: A device ‘suitable for sustained study’ is one on which a person can study at length, so ‘sustained’ here means prolonged, not financially supported.

subject: English
q: The phrase ‘company without obligation’ suggests that the library allows an elderly person to:
o: be among other people without having to do or buy anything in return
join compulsory reading groups
work there as an unpaid volunteer
avoid all contact with other visitors
explanation: The paragraph describes the library as a space ‘that asks nothing of them but a little silence’, so it offers the presence of others without any demand in return.

subject: English
q: The tone of the final sentence of the passage is best described as:
o: celebratory
sarcastic
cautionary
resigned
explanation: The sentence warns that a city closing its libraries ‘may discover, too late’ that it has lost something hard to restore, which is a warning rather than a celebration or surrender.

subject: English
q: The passage mainly describes:
o: the daily routine of shopkeepers in a bazaar
the dangers of flooding in narrow lanes
how an old city changes before, during and after a sudden rain
a family’s preparations for a festival
explanation: The four paragraphs move in order through the silent heat, the arrival of wind, the downpour and the city’s recovery once the rain has passed.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what was the first sign of the coming rain?
o: A sudden wind in the lanes
A dark cloud over the rooftops
The smell of wet earth
The cry of a corn seller
explanation: The second paragraph opens, ‘The first sign was not cloud but wind’; the smell of earth came afterwards and the corn seller appears only when the rain is over.

subject: English
q: The word ‘frantic’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: brightly coloured
neatly arranged
badly torn
wildly agitated
explanation: The washing, caught by a sudden wind, is ‘flapping like frantic flags’ — moving in a wild, agitated way.

subject: English
q: The statement that the grandmothers ‘pretended to disapprove’ suggests that they:
o: were angry that the children had disobeyed them
secretly enjoyed watching the children play in the rain
feared that the children would be hurt
did not notice the children at all
explanation: Disapproval that is only pretended is not real; the grandmothers kept up an appearance of sternness while in fact taking pleasure in the scene.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why did the walls of the houses glow after the rain?
o: The rain had washed away the dust that had hidden their colours
They had recently been repainted
The sun was brighter than it had been all day
Lamps had been lit in the lanes
explanation: The last paragraph speaks of ‘washed walls’ glowing in colours ‘that the dust had hidden for weeks’; the sun is described as ‘weaker now’, not brighter.

subject: English
q: The mood of the final paragraph is best described as:
o: lingering unease
festive excitement
restored calm
weary resignation
explanation: Familiar activity resumes — awnings go up, pigeons circle, a vendor calls — and the city is ‘given back to itself’, a mood of calm return rather than the excitement of the downpour.
